title: Clo User Story - D_Archive By Virgile Biosa
description:
Fort de son parcours en design de mode, Virgile Biosa aborde l'univers numérique avec une philosophie où le savoir-faire prime. Là où d'autres voient la 3D comme un simple raccourci, Virgile la considère comme un microscope, s'en servant pour déconstruire des patrons historiques complexes pour d_archive et concevoir des simulations hyper-réalistes pour des marques internationales.

À travers le collectif d_archive, Virgile et son équipe pénètrent dans les réserves des musées pour faire le pont entre patrimoine et innovation. En numérisant minutieusement des vêtements en voie de détérioration, qu'il s'agisse de fragiles drapés du XVIIIe siècle ou de latex vieillissant, il ne se contente pas d'archiver l'histoire : il la ressuscite. Ces patrons reconstitués sont mis à la disposition d'une nouvelle génération qui peut les télécharger, les étudier et les réinventer. Découvrez comment la technologie 3D démystifie l'artisanat du passé pour bâtir l'avenir de la mode.

With a background in fashion design, Virgile Biosa approaches the digital realm with a "craft-first" philosophy. Where others see 3D as a mere shortcut, Virgile treats it as a microscope, using it to deconstruct intricate historical patterns for d_archive and engineer hyper-realistic simulations for global brands.

Through the d_archive collective, Virgile and his team step into museum vaults to bridge the gap between heritage and innovation. By meticulously digitizing disintegrating garments, from fragile 18th-century drapes to aging latex, he isn't just archiving history; he’s resurrecting it. These reconstructed patterns are made accessible for a new generation to download, study, and redesign. Discover how 3D technology is demystifying the craftsmanship of the past to build the future of fashion.
transcript: Hello, my name is Virgil Biosa and I am a 3D artist. I started my studies in a fashion school, it was in Belgium, in Saint-Luc, in Tournai, and I did a master's degree at the UPR school in Paris. This is where I discovered 3D in an internship where I did 3D prototyping and design visualization on Clo. And by entering this internship, this is where I really wanted to experiment with all these Clo tools for creation of clothes, by integrating techniques of motion capture to put in animation and it is there that I really discovered this world. After my studies, I started to work directly with brands, doing prototyping, design, visualization, that kind of thing. And at the same time, my ambition was to continue to do visual experimentation with all the tools that were really new to me. On Clo I was able to discover, better understand and better understand patronage, I understand how to modify a shirt, how to visualize, how to do all this with the 3D model. I used the 3D model in the class of 3D. fell, this kind of thing. I think that's where it brought me a lot. In a quasi-daily way, I use Claw for about all my projects because I have a little more than one cap, so sometimes I'm going to call you to do prototyping, sometimes it's going to be to do advertising campaigns and suddenly I intervene after more than two years have passed. I do the clothes in Claw 3D, I do the simulation, I export the renders, etc. Or if it's more creative, we can really manipulate the fabric in real time, make a lot of couple variations. It's pretty cool because you can see the evolution, so you can always go back and see the progression. And in fact, since it's real time, when I change a curve, it directly impacts my silhouette, so it's pretty natural in itself. It's straightforward. The D-Archive project is a project that I co-founded with three colleagues and friends who are Italian, so they are Martina Ponzoni, Eriza Ibrahimi and Daniele Scalente. We all had this idea in our heads to bring back to light the pieces of art so that in 20 years, 30 years, it will still be consultable. And we propose to digitize the archives of schools and museums to make them accessible in priority to students and also to designers, researchers, some historians, etc. When we go to a museum, for example, in the archives, and we open a box and we discover the clothes, we will often put on the little white gloves and we will go out with precision the piece and we will start to take all the measurements by hand, take all the technical information and put it in place. I had to transvase them in Clo3D to then assemble the piece in 3D and I also had to take back the Clo files once they were finished, add all the hard traces, all the overpictures, the embroidery, make it as realistic as possible and render them. A tool like Clo to be able to manipulate them without touching them in real life, see how it was worn, how it fell, how it will also be impacted by the movement, a moving body, if someone walks, if someone runs, etc. It will impact the garment in different ways and it will be interesting to be able to do all these simulations digitally. We can have parts that are very worn, either the fabric will be unwashed, or indeed there are parts that will be torn or missing pieces. For example, we just find a pocket or just a piece of belt or just the top of the garment and the bottom is totally disintegrated. And from there, we can imagine what it looks like and redraw the pattern. Last year, we worked with Clo, we worked with Clo, we worked with Clo, we worked for a museum. We digitized a silhouette of a Belgian creator whose large part was made of latex. And after 10 years, the latex started to turn white and frown. So we made a 3D interface and the idea is to show a before and after and be able to switch between the two modes. And it's quite interesting because we created a whole interface on which we can zoom in, click on points of interest and have information on how the costume was glued in latex, how each element of the silhouette was made, etc. For now, on our website, we can have access to a gallery with all the pieces that we have digitized, have contextual information on when the piece was made, in what context, why, by whom. So the idea is to have a digital way that we can consult directly online and download to be able to assemble the piece on Clo 3D and create new things from there. It's super interesting, it creates a kind of community and it's pretty cool. In the field of research, there are a lot of possibilities. In the field of research, design, or in any case creative prospecting, it's still a super fast tool. We tested a lot of variations before deciding on one. And apart from that, it also allowed me to demystify a lot of things around patronage. Especially with The Archive, it really allows me to understand how the patterns are made, where they were made, and how to rebuild them today. And we quickly got results that work well. So that's how we found a really good product. Thanks for watching. We hope you learned something. Remember to subscribe to our channel, and to click that bell icon, and to turn on notifications to get notifications when new videos are posted. Thanks again for watching and have a great day!
markdown_content: ## Background: Virgil Biosa’s training and discovery of Clo Virgil Biosa is a 3D artist who began his studies in a fashion school in Belgium (Saint-Luc, in Tournai) and later completed a master’s degree at UPR School in Paris. He first discovered 3D during an internship focused on 3D prototyping and design visualization on Clo, where he wanted to experiment with Clo tools for creating clothes. In that internship, he explored integrating motion capture techniques into animation. This is where he “really discovered” the broader workflow and possibilities around digital garment creation. After finishing his studies, he began working directly with brands on prototyping and design visualization, while continuing visual experimentation with newly learned tools. ## Using Clo 3D for garment prototyping, simulation, and real-time fabric manipulation Biosa describes Clo 3D as a near-daily tool across many project types, including prototyping and advertising campaigns. He notes that after more than two years of use, his typical workflow includes creating clothes in Clo 3D, running simulations, and exporting renders. He also highlights Clo 3D’s ability to enable creative, real-time fabric manipulation. By changing parameters such as curves, he can immediately see how the garment’s silhouette changes—making iteration feel “natural” and straightforward. Because the changes are real time, he can review the evolution of a design and revert to earlier stages to compare progression. For simulations, he emphasizes how Clo supports understanding garment behavior under movement. In his view, digital simulation helps designers study how garments fall, how they look when worn, and how they react to different body motions (for example, walking versus running). He also mentions working with worn or damaged garment conditions, where parts may be unwashed, torn, missing, or partially intact. ## Patronage and pattern modification with Clo 3D This section covers how Clo 3D supports patronage understanding and practical shirt modification. Biosa explains that Clo helps him better understand patronage and how to modify garments (such as a shirt) using a 3D model. He uses the 3D model to visualize and work through garment construction details. The key idea is that Clo allows pattern-related changes to be tested and visualized digitally, rather than relying only on physical iteration. He also frames Clo as a tool that helps demystify garment construction: with the right workflow, he can understand how patterns are made and how they can be rebuilt or adapted for modern use. ## D_Archive: digitizing school and museum garment archives for long-term access D_Archive is a digitization project co-founded by Virgil Biosa with three Italian colleagues and friends: Martina Ponzoni, Eriza Ibrahimi, and Daniele Scalente. The group’s goal is to bring art and garment pieces back into visibility so they remain consultable in 20–30 years. They propose digitizing archives from schools and museums to make garments accessible—prioritizing students and also designers, researchers, historians, and others who need archival access. Their approach is inspired by the museum process: when opening an archive box and discovering clothing, curators often use white gloves, examine the piece precisely, and take measurements and technical information by hand. ## End-to-end workflow: from measurements and Clo3D assembly to realistic digital rendering This section explains how physical archival information is converted into Clo 3D models and then rendered realistically. Biosa describes that after taking measurements and technical details from the physical garment, they must “transvase” (transfer) this information into Clo 3D to assemble the piece in 3D. They also take Clo files back after completion to add details and “hard traces,” including overpictures, embroidery, and other elements needed to make the final digital garment as realistic as possible. After adding those details, they render the results. A key benefit of using Clo is that it enables manipulation of garments without handling them physically. This allows digital study of how garments fall, how they were worn, and how they respond to motion—such as how a moving body changes the garment’s appearance. ## Reconstructing worn or incomplete garments and redrawing patterns digitally This section covers how D_Archive handles damaged or partially missing garments during reconstruction. Biosa explains that garments in archives can be very worn due to conditions like unwashed fabric, torn components, or missing pieces. Sometimes only a portion remains—such as a pocket, a belt piece, or the top of the garment—while the bottom is fully disintegrated. In those cases, the team reconstructs what the garment likely looked like and redraws patterns to rebuild the missing parts digitally. They use Clo-based digital workflows to test and simulate the reconstructed garment behavior and appearance. ## Case study: Belgian creator silhouette with latex and a “before/after” interface This section describes a project with a museum where Clo was used to digitize a garment made largely of latex. The team digitized the silhouette of a Belgian creator whose garment’s latex had changed over time: after 10 years, the latex started to turn white and frown (deform/warp). They created a 3D interface that supports switching between two modes: a “before” state and an “after” state. The interface includes features such as zooming in, clicking on points of interest, and viewing information about how the costume was glued in latex and how each element of the silhouette was constructed. ## Accessing digitized archives online and using downloads to build in Clo 3D This section explains how D_Archive presents digitized pieces online and supports downstream use in Clo 3D. On their website, users can access a gallery of digitized pieces along with contextual information, including when the piece was made, the context of its use, and details about who made it and why. The long-term goal is to provide digital consultation directly online and enable downloads so users can assemble the pieces in Clo 3D and create new work from the digitized assets. ## Research and design value: rapid experimentation and pattern reconstruction This section summarizes how Clo and D_Archive support research, design, and creative exploration. Biosa emphasizes that in research and design prospecting, Clo remains a very fast tool. He notes that they tested many variations before deciding on final versions, enabling efficient iteration. He also states that the Archive approach helps him understand garment construction in practical terms—specifically how patterns are made, where they were made, and how they can be rebuilt today. He reports that the team quickly achieved results that worked well, leading them to identify a strong product fit for their needs.
